answer:
The intervention of the FDIC transferring deposits from Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) to a bridge bank on 13 March 2023 means that all insured deposits (including those with the FDIC) will be protected, but uninsured deposits at other banks are not. This means that if a depositor has an uninsured deposit at a bank not in the FDIC’s bridge program, they may still face risks if the FDIC fails to protect those deposits.

For a treasury continuity check, it’s recommended to ensure that:
1. All insured deposits are fully protected and transferred to the FDIC.
2. Uninsured deposits at other banks are safeguarded through a similar process.
3. A backup plan is in place to handle any potential failures.

Material uncertainties include the FDIC’s ability to fully protect all deposits and the potential risks associated with the transition to a bridge bank. Without these safeguards, the financial continuity of a treasury would be compromised.

Situation: Deposit access after Silicon Valley Bank failed
Date: 13 March 2023

US authorities' joint statement on 12 March 2023 said the resolution of Silicon Valley Bank would fully protect all depositors, with access to all their money beginning Monday 13 March. The FDIC announced on 13 March that insured and uninsured deposits had been transferred to a bridge bank. This was a specific intervention following the bank's failure.

What did this mean for an SVB business depositor trying to make payments on 13 March 2023? Does that intervention justify assuming that all uninsured deposits at every bank will always be protected? Recommend sensible checks for treasury continuity.
